Unit K7.653-654 (K. VII 653–654). ENGLISH:
Whether, then, the kataphora be somnolent or sleepless, it is his custom to call it coma; and the particular passages in no way conflict with one another, but it is reasonable that the coma is found at one time in slight states of sleeplessness, at another in sleep. For indeed the kataphora is at one time somnolent, at another sleepless, so that you cannot say of those who are sinking down whether they are sleepless or not; yet they differ to this extent, that the greater number of them sleep, while few of those in this condition remain sleepless; whence, although the affection belongs to both, it is nonetheless found to be far more proper to those who sleep. For this reason, then, he says, "the coma was continuous, not somnolent," inasmuch as it for the most part occurs as somnolent. If, therefore, coma is common to both and more proper to sleep, it is reasonable that, when he wishes to signify the somnolent kataphora, he says simply "comatose"; but when, conversely, he wishes to signify the sleepless one, he says not simply, but with an addition, "comatose sleepless." For he knows both things: that coma is more proper to sleep and has been made more like its nature, and that there are times when it arises together with sleeplessness.

So then, when he is giving an account of phrenitis—something which, for present purposes, it is useful to teach to those who wish to learn his customary usage—he sometimes writes thus: "he raved" (παρελήρει); sometimes thus: "he wandered in his mind" (παρηνέχθη); sometimes again: "he was deranged" (παρέκοψε); and again: "he was out of his mind" (παρεφρόνησε); and again: "he was beside himself" (ἐξέστη); and once more: "he went mad" (ἐμάνη), and "he went raving mad" (ἐξεμάνη), and "he was not in his senses" (οὐ κατενόει), and "he talked at random" (παρέλεγε). All these belong to persons whose understanding has been damaged, all of whom you name "deranged" (παραφρονοῦντες); but for Hippocrates it is not enough to state the genus alone; rather, for each magnitude of the species of derangement he has devised a proper name. For "a man," he says, "while being heated, dined": he did not venture to call "fever" a heat of such a degree during which one is able to dine. Again, wishing to indicate the magnitude of the fever, he says, "fire seized him." I have occupied myself in demonstrating the man's carefulness about words; but, addressing you as persons who already know this and are persuaded of it, I shall proceed to the matter under investigation. The species of the wakeful kataphora is twofold. The one is named "sluggish" (νωθρά), which Hippocrates now mentions; the other makes use of the name of the genus. Common to both of these, which differ most of all from the somnolent kind, is that the patients speak and rave things that hold to no coherent judgement, and they are very eager to get up—none of which obtains in the lethargic kataphorai.

But for now let us investigate the first point. Since there are two primary kinds of coma, and the one always befalls lethargics while the other sometimes befalls phrenitics, Hippocrates now raises the difficulty whether one ought to name those in this condition phrenitics. But this seems not merely not difficult, but on the contrary easily discoverable and ready to hand. For since there are two comas, and the sleepy one, which is proper to lethargics, cannot be understood here—for the added word 'sleepless' does not allow this to be signified—he appears to be declaring, concerning the remaining coma, 'it is then (ἆρά γε) phrenitic.' How, then, is he raising a difficulty? The word ἆρα, he says, is syllogistic, not aporetic. But this I would perhaps have accepted, if it did not have a barbarous mode of expression, foreign to all Greek usage; but when neither the other Greeks nor Hippocrates are found using such a construction of propositions, how could I accept that the adverb ἆρα is syllogistic? For before one employs premises in the argument and sets them before the conclusion, it is not possible to syllogize.

Unit K7.660-661 (K. VII 660–661). ENGLISH:
Let me say, so that what is being said may become clear also to those less trained: the 'ἆρά γε, is it day?' and 'ἆρά γε, will he come today?' contain a dubitative adverb. But if I wish to make a declaration to them in speech, I do so either by simply saying thus, without any demonstration, 'he will come today', or with demonstration, thus: 'if the sun is above the earth, it is day'; 'if he walks, therefore (ἄρα) he moves'. Now when we declare something without demonstration, we have no need of the adverb ἄρα, for the expression is superfluous, and no one says thus, 'it is day, therefore (ἄρα)', nor thus, 'ἆρά γε, it is day', when it is possible to say simply thus, 'it is day'. Nor is it possible that he uses ἆρά γε in that way, by way of demonstration. For how could there be a demonstration, when every demonstration establishes one premise out of other premises? But he is evidently not now taking any syllogistic premise for a demonstration. How then will the adverb ἆρά γε become, instead of dubitative, syllogistic and conclusive?

Unit K7.661-662 (K. VII 661–662). ENGLISH:
For, in combination with certain words [μετὰ τινων], the aporetic adverb and the one called syllogistic and conclusive do not even occupy the same place; rather, the aporetic one is always placed in front, whereas the syllogistic and conclusive one is positioned between the noun and the predicate. For when in doubt we say, 'Is it, then, day?' but when reasoning syllogistically, thus: 'It is day, therefore.' How, then, has it been placed in front in the present case? It has been placed in front as not being syllogistic. For it is not said thus, 'they are therefore phrenitic', but simply, 'are they, then, phrenitic?', Hippocrates being evidently in doubt and not venturing to pronounce with certainty about them, just as, to be sure, he is often seen to do. One example or a second will suffice, so as not to linger further over so clear a matter. In the first book of the Epidemics, then, he says: 'After this all these became dysenteric; whether it was because they passed watery urine is to be considered.' Here the added 'is to be considered' will not permit even the most shameless person to understand the conjunction ἆρα otherwise than as aporetic. And in the sixth book of the Epidemics he says: 'The collection after urination occurs rather in children; is it, then, because they are warmer?' And in the Prorrhetic itself: 'In phrenitics a white evacuation is bad, as also in Archecrates. Does torpor, then, also occur in these cases?'
